title: The Twelve-Month Rule Does Not Describe a New Fab - Semiwiki
gist: Nikhil Shah tests the standard twelve-month capex-to-capacity assumption against five US advanced-node greenfield projects (TSMC, Intel, Samsung, Micron) and finds a median construction-to-first-production lag of 45 months, range 39-60. His argument: the twelve-month rule describes brownfield tool installs, not new fabs, and capex announcements must be labeled greenfield vs. brownfield and tied to a disclosed wafer-start figure before they can be used as a supply signal.

themes.theme: Two clocks: brownfield tools vs. greenfield fabs

insights.claim: Across five US advanced-node greenfield projects covering TSMC, Intel, Samsung and Micron, disclosed schedules show a median construction-start-to-first-production lag of 45 months with a range of 39 to 60 months.
insights.so_what: A 45-month median means today's greenfield capex lands as supply around 2030 — a direct input to any semiconductor supply/demand model.
insights.quote: Measured from the start of construction to first production, the disclosed schedules have a median lag of 45 months and a range of 39 to 60 months.
insights.locator: I tested the distinction using five advanced-node projects
insights.speaker: Admin

insights.claim: The twelve-month capex-to-capacity lag is a reasonable working assumption only for equipment installed in an existing fab, where the shell, cleanroom, utilities and workforce are already in place and the delay is procurement, installation and qualification.
insights.so_what: Separating the two clocks prevents double-counting capacity: brownfield spend converts fast, greenfield spend does not.
insights.quote: The shorter clock starts after the shell, cleanroom, utilities and much of the workforce are already in place.
insights.speaker: Admin

insights.claim: For greenfield sites, construction, utility connections, cleanroom systems, equipment installation, process qualification and hiring all sit between announcement and commercial output, so tool lead time captures only part of the sequence.
insights.so_what: Explains why WFE order data is a poor proxy for new-fab capacity timing — the equipment step is the shortest link in the chain.
insights.quote: A tool lead time captures only part of that sequence.
insights.locator: The longer clock starts when a company begins a greenfield site
insights.speaker: Admin

insights.claim: The author explicitly frames the finding as reconciling two apparently contradictory beliefs rather than replacing one: a twelve-month capex lag and a four-year fab schedule can both be true simultaneously.
insights.so_what: Removes a common analytical error where forecasters pick one lag and apply it to aggregate industry capex.
insights.quote: It does show why a twelve-month capex lag and a four-year fab schedule can both be true.
insights.locator: That is not a new industry rule
insights.speaker: Admin

insights.claim: TSMC's first Arizona fab began construction in June 2021 and started high-volume N4 production in the fourth quarter of 2024, roughly a 42-month span.
insights.so_what: The only fully completed leading-edge US greenfield datapoint — the anchor for timing any other announced fab.
insights.quote: Its first fab began construction in June 2021 and started high-volume N4 production in the fourth quarter of 2024.
insights.locator: TSMC’s Arizona site makes the distinction visible
insights.speaker: Admin

insights.claim: TSMC completed the structure of its second Arizona fab in 2025 but targets N3 volume production only in the second half of 2027, showing that finishing a building is not the same as finishing capacity.
insights.so_what: A two-year gap between shell completion and volume output — the trap in reading construction-progress headlines as supply.
insights.quote: Finishing the building is not the same as finishing the capacity.
insights.locator: TSMC says the structure of its second Arizona fab
insights.speaker: Admin

insights.claim: Intel broke ground on its two-fab Arizona expansion in September 2021, and Fab 52 was fully operational in October 2025 while preparing to reach high-volume Intel 18A production by year-end — about four years elapsed.
insights.so_what: Independent confirmation of the ~4-year greenfield clock at a second operator, and a dated milestone for 18A HVM.
insights.quote: Fab 52 was fully operational in October 2025 and was preparing to reach high-volume Intel 18A production by year-end.
insights.locator: Intel’s Fab 52 tells a similar story
insights.speaker: Admin

insights.claim: Samsung dates its first Taylor fab groundbreaking to 2022 and said on its Q1 2026 earnings call that the fab would start operations in 2026 with mass production in 2027; its second Taylor fab is expected to begin construction by end-2026 targeting mass production in 2030.
insights.so_what: Samsung's second Taylor fab implies a four-year clock again — 2026 construction to 2030 output — useful for out-year foundry supply models.
insights.quote: Its second Taylor fab is expected to begin construction by the end of 2026 and target mass production in 2030.
insights.locator: Samsung and Micron provide the forward-looking observations
insights.speaker: Admin

insights.claim: Micron formally announced construction start on its Boise memory fab in October 2023 and schedules initial DRAM output for 2027.
insights.so_what: Sets the date when incremental US DRAM supply actually reaches the market — relevant to memory cycle timing.
insights.quote: Micron formally announced the start of construction on its Boise memory fab in October 2023 and schedules initial DRAM output for 2027.
insights.locator: Samsung and Micron provide the forward-looking observations
insights.speaker: Admin

themes.theme: Disclosure quality as the real constraint

insights.claim: Fab milestones are not standardized: groundbreaking ceremony, start of continuous construction, structure completion, equipment move-in and volume production are different events that companies report inconsistently.
insights.so_what: Any capacity model built on press-release dates inherits definitional noise measured in years, not quarters.
insights.quote: A groundbreaking ceremony, the start of continuous construction, structure completion, equipment move-in and volume production are different events, but companies do not always report each one.
insights.speaker: Admin

insights.claim: Micron illustrates the definitional problem directly: it held a Boise groundbreaking in 2022 but issued an explicit construction-initiation release in October 2023, and choosing the ceremony date instead would lengthen the same project's measured lag by about a year.
insights.so_what: A single date-definition choice moves a project lag by ~25% — the reason cross-company lag comparisons are unreliable.
insights.quote: Using the ceremony instead would lengthen the same project’s lag by about a year.
insights.speaker: Admin

insights.claim: The author caveats his own result heavily: five projects are too few, several dates are precise only to a year, three production dates were still targets as of August 2026, and future delays would lengthen those observations.
insights.so_what: Treat 45 months as a description of a small disclosed sample, not a forecast — and note the bias is toward longer, not shorter.
insights.quote: 45 months should be read as a description of this small disclosed sample, not a forecast with false precision.
insights.locator: The sample also mixes two completed projects
insights.speaker: Admin

themes.theme: Capex-per-wafer cannot be computed from disclosures

insights.claim: TSMC's May 2020 Arizona announcement paired approximately $12 billion of spending with 20,000 wafers per month, equal to $600,000 of announced investment per monthly wafer start — the only row in the register that cleanly supports a capital-intensity calculation.
insights.so_what: A rare clean benchmark for leading-edge capital intensity: ~$600k per monthly wafer start.
insights.quote: That equals $600,000 of announced investment per monthly wafer start.
insights.locator: The capex-to-capacity ratio is harder to calculate
insights.speaker: Admin

insights.claim: More recent disclosures cannot be converted to capital intensity: Intel's original $20 billion Arizona figure covered Fab 52 and Fab 62 together with no published wafer-start target, Micron's roughly $15 billion Boise figure spans spending through the end of the decade, and TSMC's Arizona commitment now covers six logic fabs, two advanced-packaging facilities and an R&D center.
insights.so_what: Headline site investment numbers are program-scale markers, not capacity math — dividing them by wafer capacity requires undisclosed assumptions.
insights.quote: None of those figures can be divided by a single fab’s capacity without adding assumptions that the companies did not disclose.
insights.locator: More recent disclosures usually do not
insights.speaker: Admin

insights.claim: A site-level investment number measures the scale of a program but is not automatically a measure of incremental wafer capacity.
insights.so_what: Guards against the common error of treating national/site subsidy headlines as capacity additions.
insights.quote: A site-level investment number is useful for measuring the scale of a program. It is not automatically a measure of incremental wafer capacity.
insights.speaker: Admin

insights.claim: The actionable rule is that a capex announcement needs two labels before it can serve as a supply signal: whether the spending is greenfield or brownfield, and whether the disclosed dollars can be tied to a specific capacity figure.
insights.so_what: A two-question screen to apply to every fab capex headline before it enters a supply model.
insights.quote: A capex announcement needs two labels before it can be used as a supply signal: whether the spending is greenfield or brownfield, and whether the disclosed dollars can be tied to a specific capacity figure.
insights.locator: What forecasters can take from the register
insights.speaker: Admin

insights.claim: Combining brownfield and greenfield lags into a single aggregate industry capex lag hides the difference between roughly twelve months and roughly four years, systematically distorting supply forecasts.
insights.so_what: Explains recurring forecast misses on when announced fab capacity actually hits the market.
insights.quote: Combining the two in one aggregate lag hides the difference.
insights.locator: For existing fabs, a roughly twelve-month equipment lag
insights.speaker: Admin
